chunks: As-Sayyid al-Sharif says: I say: And this sermon
perhaps those with no knowledge of it attribute it to Mu'awiya, but it is the speech of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) about which there is no doubt,
and where is gold compared to dust! and sweet water compared to bitter!
and the skilful guide has pointed to that, and the expert critic 'Amr ibn Bahr al-Jahiz has critiqued it;
for he mentioned this sermon in his book
and mentioned those who attributed it to Mu'awiya,
then he spoke after it with words in its meaning, the gist of which is that he said: And this speech is more akin to the speech of Ali (peace be upon him),
and more fitting with his method of categorizing people and in the reports about what they are upon in terms of subjugation and humiliation, and with modesty and fear.
He said: And when did we find Mu'awiya in any state conducting himself in his speech with the manner of the ascetics, and the beliefs of the worshippers!
ai.seo_question: Who attributed this sermon to Mu'awiya and how did al-Jahiz refute it?
ai.summary: Sharif al-Radi defends the attribution of this sermon to Imam Ali (AS) by leveraging al-Jahiz’s literary analysis, which contrasts Ali’s consistent asceticism with Mu'awiya’s political pragmatism. This scholarly endorsement highlights the sermon's authenticity through stylistic coherence with Ali’s known character of modesty and strategic concealment (Taqiyyah). The passage serves as a definitive refutation of the 'Gold vs. Dust' dichotomy, affirming the superiority of the Ahl al-Bayt's spiritual depth over the Umayyad elite.

en.sayed-ali-raza: Some ignorant persons attributed this sermon to Mu‘āwiyah but it is the speech of Amīr al-mu’minīn. There should be no doubt about it.
What comparison is there between gold and clay or sweet and bitter water.
This has been pointed out by the skilful guide and the expert critic ‘Amr ibn Bahr al-Jahiz
as he has mentioned this sermon in his book,
(vol. 2, pp. 59-61). He has also mentioned who attributed it to Mu‘āwiyah
and then states that it is most akin to be the speech of ‘Ali
and most in accord with his way of categorising people and information about their oppression, disgrace, apprehension and fear.
(On the other hand) we never found Mu‘āwiyah in his speech, to behave the behaviour of the ascetics and to adopt the beliefs of the servants (of Allāh).
